key_concepts.summary: Sparring is not just conditioning. It is a high-risk contact load that must be tracked separately.
Technical sparring, body sparring, controlled sparring, and hard sparring are not interchangeable.
Fight camp should move from general preparation to specific preparation, sparring peak, taper, fight week, and post-fight recovery.
Fight-week training should preserve timing and sharpness while reducing accumulated fatigue and contact risk.
Headache, dizziness, visual symptoms, confusion, unusual fatigue, or worsening hand pain should override planned contact.
Post-fight training should not immediately return to normal camp load without symptom and tissue recovery checks.

technical_models.goal: Reduce fatigue and contact exposure while preserving timing, speed, mobility, and tactical confidence.

tactical_rules.rule: Do not prescribe hard sparring as default training.
Contact progression requires stance, guard, defense, partner discipline, coach control, and readiness.
Head symptoms, dizziness, confusion, or visual symptoms stop contact and require medical review.
The day after high-contact or high-intensity sparring should bias recovery or low-contact skill.
Fight-week taper should reduce contact and fatigue while retaining speed, timing, and tactical sharpness.
Avoid heavy neck/shoulder fatigue before high-contact sparring.
Aggressive dehydration or rapid weight-cut instructions should not be generated.
Post-fight return should progress from symptom-free low-contact work before sparring.

physical_demands.quality: Aerobic base for recovery between exchanges and rounds.
Repeat high-intensity exchanges without technical collapse.
Neck and trunk control under contact and fatigue context.
Maintain guard and punching quality under round fatigue.
Tolerate combined skill, sparring, S&C, conditioning, recovery, and weight-management load.
Preserve speed, timing, and reactivity while reducing fatigue.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Head contact and cumulative sparring exposure carry concussion/head-trauma risk.
High impact volume can overload hand and wrist.
Sparring plus high shoulder/neck training can increase fatigue and vulnerability.
Weight-cut stress can reduce readiness, cognition, hydration, and recovery.
Large partner skill, size, or intensity mismatch increases contact risk.
Camp fatigue can accumulate across contact, conditioning, strength, sleep, and stress.

training_implications.summary: Athlete state should store sparring rounds, intensity, head contact, symptoms, and readiness.
AI output should specify if a boxing session is no-contact, touch, technical, controlled, or open sparring.
Macro plans should know if user is in general prep, camp, sparring peak, taper, or post-fight recovery.
Readiness and symptoms should modify contact before modifying all exercise.
Use bag, pads, roadwork, intervals, and non-contact drills to condition without excess head contact.
Concussion symptoms, severe pain, or aggressive weight making require professional review.
